patient.chief_complaint: Burning pain in both feet and lower legs, severe at night, for 18 months
patient.history_present_illness: Marjorie Delacroix is a 52-year-old career diplomat with an 18-month history of progressively worsening neuropathic pain in her bilateral feet and lower legs. The pain is burning and lancinating in quality, significantly worse at night (allodynia to bedsheets), and interferes severely with her sleep. She has been unable to tolerate most footwear. She rates the pain as 8/10 on average and 10/10 at night. She has had several overseas postings, most recently 3 years in West Africa (2019-2022) and 18 months in South Asia (2022-2023). She received multiple vaccinations prior to posting including rabies series, meningococcal, typhoid, hepatitis A/B, and yellow fever. She has completed multiple antibiotic and antimalarial prophylaxis courses including dapsone, chloroquine, mefloquine, and a 9-month course of leflunomide for rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed 4 years ago. She takes methotrexate 15 mg weekly and leflunomide 20 mg daily for RA. Her current rheumatologist noted that her RA is in remission. She is very concerned that her medications may be causing nerve damage. She notes her symptoms began approximately 6 months after starting leflunomide. She has no diabetes and no alcohol use. Her prior neurologist attributed symptoms to 'stress' after NCS was interpreted as normal 1 year ago — she brings a copy of that NCS for review.

specialized_test.impression: NORMAL NCS/EMG. Large fiber motor and sensory nerve conduction studies within normal limits bilaterally. output.impression: Skin punch biopsy at proximal thigh (10 cm above iliac crest) and distal leg (10 cm above lateral malleolus). IENFD immunostaining with anti-PGP9.5 antibody.

QSART bilateral feet: absent (0 uL, reference >0.40 uL). QSART bilateral legs: severely reduced. Thermoregulatory sweat test: absent sweating bilateral feet and lower legs (anhidrosis). HRV: mildly reduced. Orthostatic vitals: no orthostatic hypotension. Findings confirm severe postganglionic sudomotor failure (small fiber/autonomic neuropathy) in bilateral lower extremities.

results.citation: Martin K et al. (2007) Peripheral neuropathy with leflunomide: a systematic review. Ann Rheum Dis 66:889-895.
results.summary: Leflunomide-associated peripheral neuropathy reported in 0.3-1% of patients; primarily axonal but small fiber cases reported; onset typically 6-24 months after initiation; reversible in 50-70% after discontinuation with cholestyramine washout; cases at therapeutic plasma levels document idiosyncratic mechanism.

results.citation: Bandyopadhyay D et al. (2020) Small fiber neuropathy from leflunomide: case series. J Neurol 267:1208-1214.
results.summary: Small fiber phenotype (normal large fiber NCS + reduced IENFD) documented in leflunomide neuropathy cases; cholestyramine washout accelerates drug elimination; 60% partial to complete pain improvement at 6 months post-discontinuation.

output.interpretation: Published evidence documents leflunomide-associated peripheral neuropathy including small fiber phenotype. Case series report improvement following drug discontinuation with accelerated elimination. Population-level response data summarized above. Clinical correlation recommended.

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Leflunomide is associated with peripheral and small-fiber neuropathy; cholestyramine washout 8 g TID x 11 days eliminates active metabolite (teriflunomide)

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is a cortical test and is non-contributory in peripheral nerve disease.
Head/brain CT has no role in peripheral neuropathy evaluation.
Brain MRI is not indicated in typical distal symmetric polyneuropathy without CNS signs.
Advanced cerebral imaging (PET/MRA/MRV/perfusion) has no routine role in peripheral neuropathy.
Echocardiography is not indicated unless cardiac amyloid is suspected.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated unless there is syncope or symptomatic dysautonomia with arrhythmia concern.

sequence_constraints.reason: Tier the workup — basic labs first, then targeted electrodiagnostic and tissue studies.

critical_actions: Recognize the small-fiber phenotype (burning pain, normal EMG/NCS, preserved reflexes/proprioception)
Skin biopsy for IENFD is the diagnostic gold standard [Lauria_2010]
Autonomic testing (QSART, HRV) to define small-fiber involvement and dysautonomia
Identify and discontinue offending drug (leflunomide); consider cholestyramine washout to accelerate elimination
contraindicated_actions: Do not stop the workup at normal EMG/NCS — small-fiber neuropathy is invisible to standard NCS
Do not continue leflunomide once SFN is documented and other causes are excluded
key_reasoning_points: Normal large-fiber exam + burning distal pain = consider small-fiber neuropathy
Normal EMG/NCS does NOT exclude small-fiber neuropathy — need skin biopsy IENFD or QSART
Drug history is essential; leflunomide is a recognized cause of toxic neuropathy

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: RA in remission with neuropathy onset after leflunomide initiation favors drug toxicity over disease activity.
